lines.text: Kesting Pass is a mile of rock and ice with Halvard's keep at the top. For forty years the Old Bear had held it against the Pale. Now he would hold it against the King.
Stane's vanguard came up the pass at dawn. Six thousand men in crimson, with forty bought lords at the front, their rings blazing like a field of candles.
Pretty, aren't they? Like candles on a cake. Let's blow them out.
I couldn't fight. Everyone knew that. So I stood on the keep's highest tower, behind the line, and did the only thing I could. I felt.

Two thousand threads ran out from me into the pass, and every one was a person. When a thread went sharp, I knew where, and how badly, and I sent help. I could feel the whole battle, like a hand inside a glove.
The beacons told us where Stane would turn. The glass-steel told his lords what we thought of their rings.
Their fire went out at the first touch. A bought lord without his aether is just a man in very expensive armour, looking very surprised.
Lord Stane. We've met. You may remember. You spent most of it on the ground.
Hale. You drunken disgrace. This time I'll finish you.
Oswin's glass-steel took the fire off Stane's sword in one stroke. Stane looked at his bare blade, then at Oswin. Then he ran.
Again? Ashby's still waiting, you coward!
Then the Wolfhound Riders came over the ridge out of the snow, down the one slope nobody guards, because nothing can climb it.
Wren on Tarn, Kell on Rook, and fourteen frost-wolves with names like Biscuit, roaring. Stane's flank folded like wet paper.
By the middle of the afternoon, the royal vanguard was running back down the pass and leaving its banners in the snow. We had won.
And then I felt the first one go dark.
Not sharp. Not hurt. Gone, the way Dunn's had gone. A boy from Saltmouth, on the lower wall.
Then another. Then another. All afternoon, while the battle was being won, they went out one by one, like lamps in a house where someone walks from room to room.
I counted. I couldn't stop counting.
We held, boy! The pass is ours! Do you hear them cheering? Boy?
I heard them. Halvard's men were cheering. Wren's riders were howling with the wolves. Somebody was singing.
I stood on the tower with my hands on the cold stone, and finished counting.
Twenty.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and twenty-nine, coming soon.
